entries.meaning: The reduced going to of the future. ---
examples: I'm gonna call her back in a minute.
It's gonna rain before we get home.
What are you gonna do about it?
entries.русский: собираюсь, буду (сокращение от going to — только о будущем)
entries.expands to: going to, the future marker only
entries.type: informal — a spoken reduction, written only in dialogue, texts and lyrics
entries.register: informal — universal in American speech, out of place in anything edited
entries.question form: You gonna eat that? — in a casual question the are vanishes along with the reduction; the full form is Are you going to eat that?
entries.contrast: Gonna is only the future going to. When going to means literal movement it never reduces: I'm going to the store stays as it is, and ✗ I'm gonna the store is not English. The test is simple — a verb has to follow (gonna leave, gonna rain, gonna be fine), never a noun or a place. Compare wanna, which has the mirror-image rule.

entries.meaning: The reduced want to before a verb. ---
examples: I wanna leave before the traffic starts.
Do you wanna come with us?
She doesn't wanna talk about it yet.
entries.русский: хочу, хочешь (сокращение от want to)
entries.type: informal — a spoken reduction, written only in dialogue, texts and lyrics
entries.register: informal — heard in nearly every conversation, never used in edited prose
entries.question form: Wanna grab lunch? — the whole Do you is dropped, which is the ordinary American way of proposing something.
entries.contrast: Wanna is want to and nothing else, so a verb has to follow: I wanna go, but ✗ I wanna a coffee. In speech I want a coffee reduces to almost the same sound, yet it is written want a — the noun version has no wanna spelling. There is a second, subtler block: when a subject stands between the two words, the reduction is impossible. Who do you want to win? cannot become ✗ Who do you wanna win?, because who is the subject of win.

entries.meaning: gotta stands for 2 different things.
examples: I gotta go — my bus leaves in five minutes.
You gotta see the new place, it's enormous.
We gotta be at the airport by six.
I gotta friend who does exactly this kind of work.
You gotta minute? I need to ask you something.
He's gotta new job downtown.

senses.head: Obligation — the reduced have got to
examples: I gotta go — my bus leaves in five minutes.
You gotta see the new place, it's enormous.
We gotta be at the airport by six.

senses.head: Possession — the reduced have got a, with the article already inside it
examples: I gotta friend who does exactly this kind of work.
You gotta minute? I need to ask you something.
He's gotta new job downtown.

entries.русский: надо, должен; а также «есть у меня» (от have got to и have got a)
entries.expands to: have got to or have got a
entries.type: informal — a spoken reduction of the two uses of have got
entries.register: informal — normal in speech, written only in dialogue and texts
entries.ambiguity: Two different sentences reduce to the same gotta. Before a verb it is got to and means obligation: I gotta go is I have got to go. Before a noun the final -a is itself the article a: I gotta minute is I have got a minute. That is why ✗ I gotta a minute? is wrong — it writes the article twice.
entries.question form: Gotta minute? — the Have you is dropped completely. The full form is Have you got a minute?
entries.contrast: Gotta reduces have got, never the past tense got: I got a letter yesterday has nothing to do with it. Americans usually drop the have as well (I gotta go, rarely I've gotta go), which is fine in speech; in writing use have to or have got to. Compare hafta, which carries the same obligation through have to.

entries.meaning: The reduced give me. ---
examples: Gimme a call when you land.
Gimme that wrench — I can reach it from here.
Gimme a second, I'm almost done.
entries.русский: дай, дай мне (сокращение от give me)
entries.type: informal — a verb fused with its object pronoun
entries.register: informal — normal in speech, blunt on paper
entries.contrast: Only me fuses this way: there is no ✗ gimme him or ✗ gimme you. Gimme has also hardened into set expressions — gimme a break is disbelief, not a request for rest, and in sports talk a gimme is a noun meaning something so easy it is granted without being played. Written out, give me is always correct.

entries.meaning: The reduced let me. ---
examples: Lemme know what time you're getting in.
Lemme see that picture again.
Lemme think about it overnight.
entries.русский: дай мне, дай-ка (сокращение от let me)
entries.type: informal — a verb fused with its object pronoun
entries.register: informal — normal in speech, out of place in edited writing
entries.contrast: Only let me reduces this way; let him and let her do not. Let us has its own contraction, let's, and that one is fully standard writing. Lemme is always followed by a bare verb: lemme know, lemme see, lemme think.

entries.meaning: The reduced (I) don't know. ---
examples: Dunno — ask Marcy, she was there.
I dunno if the store is still open.
I dunno what he wants me to say.
entries.русский: не знаю (сокращение от (I) don't know)
entries.expands to: don't know, usually with the I swallowed into it
entries.type: informal — a whole clause reduced to two syllables
entries.register: informal — speech and text messages only
entries.contrast: Dunno normally stands for the entire sentence I don't know: the subject is gone, not merely reduced. It does not conjugate, so ✗ he dunno is not the pattern in General American — for a third person say he doesn't know. In writing it reads as a shrug, which is sometimes exactly wrong in an email.

entries.meaning: The reduced kind of, both as a hedge and in its literal sense. ---
examples: I'm kinda tired — can we do this tomorrow?
That's kinda what I was afraid of.
What kinda car did she end up buying?
entries.русский: вроде, как бы, довольно (сокращение от kind of)
entries.type: informal — a preposition swallowed into the noun before it
entries.register: informal — texts and casual writing, not essays or business email
entries.contrast: The library also lists kinda as an adverb of degree, and that softening use is the commoner one: kinda tired, I kinda like him. The literal kind of reduces the same way after a noun or a question word: what kinda car is that? In edited writing, use kind of, somewhat or a little. Its twin is sorta.

entries.meaning: The reduced sort of. ---
examples: It sorta works, but not the way we planned.
I sorta promised I'd be there.
She's sorta my boss and sorta not.
entries.русский: вроде, отчасти (сокращение от sort of)
entries.type: informal — a preposition swallowed into the noun before it
entries.register: informal — texts and casual writing only
entries.contrast: Sorta and kinda are interchangeable as hedges, with kinda the commoner of the two in American speech. Neither belongs in edited prose — write sort of, somewhat, or drop the hedge altogether.

entries.meaning: The reduced out of. ---
examples: Get outta here before he sees you.
We're outta milk again.
That came outta nowhere.
entries.русский: из, вон из (сокращение от out of)
entries.type: informal — a two-word preposition run together
entries.register: informal — speech, dialogue and lyrics
entries.contrast: Outta is out of, not ought to — that one is spelled oughta and is a different word. It lives mostly in fixed phrases: get outta here, outta luck, outta nowhere, outta my way. Written out of is always available and always safe.

entries.meaning: The reduced lot of inside a lot of. ---
examples: There were a lotta people at the funeral.
That's a lotta money for a used car.
He's got a lotta nerve showing up here.
entries.русский: много (сокращение от lot of в обороте a lot of)
entries.type: informal — a quantifier phrase run together
entries.register: informal — speech and casual writing
entries.contrast: Lotta carries only the lot of part, so the article in front stays: a lotta people, not ✗ lotta people. The plural lots of reduces the same way, to lotsa. Both are speech spellings; a lot of is the written form, and alot is never a word.

entries.meaning: The reduced have to of obligation. ---
examples: I hafta be up at five tomorrow.
Do you hafta leave so early?
You don't hafta answer that.
entries.русский: надо, должен (сокращение от have to)
entries.type: informal — the obligation have to run together
entries.register: informal — the spelling is casual, the pronunciation is universal
entries.contrast: Listen for the /f/: the obligation have to is pronounced with a voiceless /f/ and /t/, which is why it is spelled hafta and not ✗ havta. The possessive have keeps its /v/ — I hafta go but I have a car. The third person reduces the same way, to hasta. Compare gotta, which delivers the same obligation through have got to.

entries.meaning: The reduced could have before a past participle. ---
examples: I coulda told you that a week ago.
We coulda been there by now if we'd left on time.
You coulda gotten hurt doing that.
entries.русский: мог бы (сокращение от could have)
entries.type: informal — a modal plus a reduced have
entries.register: informal — speech and dialogue; in writing use could have or could've
entries.contrast: Coulda is what could've actually sounds like, and it is the source of the commonest spelling mistake in American English: ✗ could of. There is no of in it — the -a is a reduced have, which is why the participle follows (coulda gone, coulda known). The set woulda, coulda, shoulda is a fixed phrase for pointless hindsight.

entries.meaning: The reduced would have before a past participle. ---
examples: I woulda called, but my phone was dead.
She woulda said something if she'd known.
That woulda been a lot easier.
entries.русский: сделал бы (сокращение от would have)
entries.type: informal — a modal plus a reduced have
entries.register: informal — speech and dialogue; in writing use would have or would've
entries.contrast: Same trap as coulda: the -a is have, never of, so ✗ would of is always an error. Woulda belongs to the unreal past — it needs a condition somewhere, stated or understood: I woulda called implies if I could have. Written out it is would have or would've.

entries.meaning: The reduced should have before a past participle. ---
examples: I shoulda known better than to trust him.
You shoulda seen his face.
We shoulda booked the earlier flight.
entries.русский: надо было, следовало (сокращение от should have)
entries.type: informal — a modal plus a reduced have
entries.register: informal — speech and dialogue; in writing use should have or should've
entries.contrast: The -a is have, so ✗ should of is an error here too. Shoulda is almost always regret about something that did not happen: I shoulda known means I did not know and wish I had. Regret about someone else's behavior comes out as blame — You shoulda called.

entries.meaning: The reduced because. ---
examples: I left early 'cause I had a headache.
We're not going, 'cause the roads are bad.
Just 'cause he said it doesn't make it true.
entries.русский: потому что (сокращение от because)
entries.type: informal — a conjunction with its first syllable gone
entries.register: informal — dialogue, lyrics and texts; write because in anything edited
entries.contrast: The apostrophe stands for the missing be-, so the careful spelling is 'cause. The same word is also written cuz, and both are equally informal. Do not confuse it with the noun cause (a reason, a purpose), which rhymes with laws and is a different word entirely: the cause of the fire has nothing to do with 'cause it was cold.

entries.meaning: The reduced because, spelled as it sounds. ---
examples: I'm staying in cuz it's freezing out.
He quit cuz they wouldn't give him weekends off.
Not cuz I want to — cuz I have to.
entries.русский: потому что (разговорное написание because)
entries.type: informal — a conjunction with its first syllable gone
entries.register: informal — texting and lyrics above all
entries.ambiguity: Cuz also writes the clipped cousin — my cuz is a relative, not a reason, and in some circles it is a friendly term of address. What follows tells you which: the conjunction takes a whole clause, the noun takes nothing.
entries.contrast: Cuz, 'cause and the British cos are three spellings of one reduced because. Cuz is the texting spelling; 'cause keeps the apostrophe that marks the missing syllable and looks slightly more careful on the page. Neither belongs in school or business writing, where the full because is the only option.

entries.meaning: The contracted you all, used as a plural you. ---
examples: Y'all want to grab something to eat after?
I'll see y'all at the game on Saturday.
All y'all need to be on the bus by seven.
entries.русский: вы, вы все (сокращение от you all; южное и афроамер.)
entries.type: dialect — the second-person plural that standard English lacks
entries.register: regional — Southern and African American English, and now widely used far beyond them
entries.contrast: The apostrophe replaces the missing letters of you, so the spelling is y'all, never ✗ ya'll. English lost its plural you when thou died, and y'all is the most successful of the forms that fill the hole, beside you guys (national), youse (northeastern) and you'uns or yinz (Pittsburgh). All y'all is not redundant: it forces the reading 'every single one of you'. The possessive is y'all's. The library also lists y'all as a personal pronoun, where its associative use — Is y'all coming Sunday? said to one person but meaning her whole household — is treated in full.

entries.meaning: The reduced you, subject or object alike. ---
examples: See ya Monday — I'll leave the keys at the desk.
I'll call ya as soon as I land.
Ya never know, it might clear up by noon.
entries.русский: ты, вы (редуцированное you)
entries.type: informal — the weak form of a pronoun, not a dialect form
entries.register: informal — the spelling is casual, though the sound is what everyone produces
entries.contrast: Ya is nothing but unstressed you written down: not Southern, not plural, not uneducated. After a /t/ or /d/ it stops being a separate syllable at all and fuses with the word before it — got you becomes gotcha, did you becomes didja, what are you becomes whatcha, bet you becomes betcha. It is never a possessive; the reduced your is yer. The library also lists ya among the personal pronouns.

entries.meaning: The unstressed them, written as it sounds. ---
examples: Just tell 'em we'll be ten minutes late.
I saw 'em leaving as I pulled in.
Round 'em up and load 'em on the truck.
entries.русский: их, им (редуцированное them)
entries.type: informal — a reduced object pronoun, leaning on the verb before it
entries.register: informal — in writing only; in speech it is simply the normal unstressed form
entries.contrast: The surprise is that 'em is not a clipping of them at all. It descends from Middle English hem, the native plural object pronoun that the Norse-borrowed them pushed out of the written language while the old form survived in the mouth. The apostrophe writes down a history nobody remembers. Fixed phrases keep it: give 'em hell, knock 'em dead, round 'em up, you can't win 'em all. When the pronoun carries stress it is always them. The library also lists 'em among the personal pronouns.

entries.meaning: The contracted of the clock, used after a number to name a whole hour. ---
examples: The store opens at nine o'clock.
It's almost three o'clock — we should get going.
I'll meet you at the station at six o'clock.
entries.русский: час, часов (о времени по часам; из of the clock)
entries.type: fixed — frozen from of the clock, the last survivor of a whole family
entries.register: standard — fully standard everywhere, in speech and in the most formal writing
entries.contrast: The apostrophe does exactly what it does in can't: it marks something missing, here the whole of of the. Nothing else survives of the old pattern — five of the clock has been gone for two centuries. Use it only with whole hours from one to twelve: at six o'clock, but at 6:30 and never ✗ 6:30 o'clock. Never combine it with a.m. or p.m. (✗ seven o'clock p.m.); say seven p.m. or seven o'clock in the evening. Russian в шесть часов is at six o'clock or simply at six. The library also lists o'clock as an adverb of time.

entries.meaning: The contracted madam, used to address a woman politely. ---
examples: Yes, ma'am, I'll have that ready by Friday.
Excuse me, ma'am — you dropped your scarf.
Can I get you anything else, ma'am?
entries.русский: мэм, мадам (вежливое обращение; сокращение от madam)
entries.type: fixed — frozen from madam
entries.register: standard — polite address, near-obligatory in the South and in the military
entries.contrast: The apostrophe replaces the -d- of madam, so the spelling is ma'am, not ✗ mam or ✗ maam. Its counterpart is sir, which is not a contraction of anything. Yes, ma'am is plain courtesy in the South, in the armed forces and in service work; in the Northeast and on the West Coast it can land badly on a younger woman, who may hear it as a comment on her age. The unreduced madam now survives only in titles like Madam President and in the salutation Dear Madam.

entries.meaning: The reduced suppose, including the supposed to of expectation. ---
examples: I s'pose so, if there's no other way.
You're not s'posed to park there.
What am I s'posed to tell her?
entries.русский: полагаю, наверное (сокращение от suppose)
entries.type: informal — a verb with its first syllable gone
entries.register: informal — dialogue and casual speech; write suppose otherwise
entries.contrast: S'pose loses the whole first syllable of suppose. It turns up in two places above all: the lukewarm agreement I s'pose so, and s'posed to, which is how supposed to actually sounds — note that the -d goes silent too. Do not mix s'posed to up with hafta and gotta: supposed to reports a rule or expectation somebody else set, and often hints that it was broken.

entries.meaning: whatcha stands for 2 different things.
examples: Whatcha doing this weekend?
Whatcha looking at?
Whatcha laughing about?
Whatcha want on your burger?
Whatcha think of the new place?

senses.head: Standing for what are you, before an -ing form
examples: Whatcha doing this weekend?
Whatcha looking at?
Whatcha laughing about?

senses.head: Standing for what do you, before a bare verb
examples: Whatcha want on your burger?
Whatcha think of the new place?

entries.русский: что ты…? (сокращение от what are you или what do you)
entries.expands to: what are you or what do you
entries.type: informal — a question word fused with its auxiliary and pronoun
entries.register: informal — speech, dialogue and lyrics only
entries.ambiguity: The same whatcha hides two different auxiliaries. Before an -ing form it is what are you: Whatcha doing? Before a bare verb it is what do you: Whatcha want? Nothing in the spelling tells you which — only the verb that follows.
entries.question form: Whatcha exists only in questions; there is no statement form. The full versions are What are you…? and What do you…?, and the ya inside it is the reduced you fusing with the /t/ before it.

entries.meaning: The reduced bet you, in predictions and in the fixed You betcha.
examples: I betcha he shows up twenty minutes late.
You betcha I'll be there.
Betcha can't guess who I ran into today.
entries.русский: спорим, точно (сокращение от bet you)
entries.type: informal — a verb fused with a reduced you
entries.register: informal — speech and dialogue
entries.contrast: Betcha is bet you with the /t/ and the /j/ of ya fused into a /tʃ/ — the same change that turns got you into gotcha and what are you into whatcha. Two patterns account for nearly all its uses: I betcha introduces a prediction, and You betcha is a fixed interjection meaning an emphatic yes, associated with the Upper Midwest and with nobody's actual wager.
